title: Niece of N.H. couple famous for alien abduction story to speak at Exeter UFO Festival - The Boston Globe
excerpt: Betty and Barney Hill reconstructed a harrowing memory of having allegedly been physically examined by gray-skinned bald humanoid beings.
content:
Kathleen Marden recalls coming home from school as a 13-year-old in Portsmouth, N.H., on Sept. 20, 1961, as her mother took an anxious phone call about an unnerving incident that would come to inspire scores of stories about purported alien encounters.

Marden’s aunt, Betty Hill, was on the line, concerned about an unidentified flying object that she and her husband, Barney Hill, had reportedly seen the night before while driving through New Hampshire’s White Mountains region after a trip to Canada.

The couple, who realized they had “lost” about two hours of time after spotting a strange hovering craft, would eventually reconstruct a harrowing memory of having allegedly been abducted and physically examined by gray-skinned bald humanoid beings.

Their story, which has been credited with shaping modern cultural perceptions of extraterrestrials and UFOs, would form the basis for magazine articles, books, TV shows, and a forthcoming Hollywood film titled “Strange Arrivals.”

But the Hills — an interracial couple who had built professional careers and a reputation as civil rights advocates in New Hampshire at a time when anti-miscegenation laws were still common in other states — reported their sighting to authorities and researchers without seeking publicity, according to Marden.

“They were very politically active and certainly did not want anyone to know about that experience,” she said in an interview. “It was released to the public as the result of a violation of confidentiality. It was devastating to Betty and Barney and to my family.”

The Hills had undergone several hypnosis therapy sessions with renowned Boston psychiatrist Benjamin Simon in 1963 and 1964 in their efforts to make sense of what happened and to grapple with their anxiety. Despite the Hills and Simon refusing to participate in coverage of their case, the Boston Traveler ran a series of stories in October 1965 that sparked a media frenzy. A New Hampshire historical marker in Lincoln commemorates the incident.

Marden, now 78, decided years after the incident to dig deeper into what her aunt and uncle experienced. She coauthored a book and is returning to the Exeter UFO Festival this weekend to speak about her research.

While the annual festival — which is based on a different famous alleged UFO sighting, the so-called “Incident at Exeter” on Sept. 3, 1965, in nearby Kensington — features a range of fun and lighthearted activities on Saturday and Sunday for kids and families, Marden said it’s also important for adults to hear about the latest developments in UFO research, and to keep an open mind.

“I’ve found many of the answers that I have been looking for,” she said, though some questions remain. “And I don’t know if I will ever find the answer to those.”
